metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
After a decade of decline, colocation rental rates are rising, signaling that demand for data center capacity has outpaced available supply.

Rate increases are a direct market signal. When prices fall steadily, it means supply exceeds what customers need. When they reverse, it means the opposite. Colocation rental rates measure the cost to lease compute capacity in specific metros, so rising rates tell you that AI workloads and other computing demand have grown faster than the buildings and power infrastructure to serve them.

For AI specifically, this matters because colocation capacity is not infinitely fungible. A customer cannot move a training run from Silicon Valley to a distant region without latency costs and operational friction. When rates rise in major hubs, it forces a choice: pay more for proximity, or accept the constraints of distant capacity. This constrains where AI development can happen in the near term.

The data does not show which metros are tightest, how much rates have risen, or whether supply is expanding to meet demand. It tracks price only, which is a lagging indicator. The actual binding constraint is whether new buildings and power can be built and connected fast enough to satisfy the demand that these rising rates confirm.
